position: both — *a friendly neighbor*, *Our neighbors are friendly*
takes: *to* or *toward* a person (how you treat them: *friendly to newcomers*); *to* a group or an idea (supportive of it: *friendly to small businesses*); *with* a person (on good terms with them: *friendly with the neighbors*)
contrast: There is no adverb *friendlily*. *She smiled friendly* is wrong; say *She smiled in a friendly way* or *She gave me a friendly smile*. After a linking verb the adjective is right: *He seems friendly*, *Be friendly*. *Friendly to* someone is about how you treat them; *friendly with* someone means you are on good terms: *I'm friendly with her brother* (мы с её братом приятели). In *user-friendly*, *eco-friendly* and *kid-friendly* the word means suitable for, or not harmful to.

senses.gloss: Kind and pleasant to other people; behaving like a friend.
examples: The people at the front desk were really *friendly*.
She has a warm, *friendly* smile.
My new coworkers are a lot *friendlier* than my old ones.

senses.gloss: On good terms with someone; not hostile.
examples: The two countries have had *friendly* relations for decades.
I'm *friendly* with a few of the other parents at school.
We parted on *friendly* terms.

senses.gloss: Supportive of a person, a group or an idea; ready to agree or help.
examples: The senator gave her speech to a *friendly* crowd of supporters.
The new mayor has been *friendly* to small businesses.
Don't expect the reviewers to be *friendly* to a sequel.

senses.gloss: Of a place or atmosphere: welcoming and comfortable.
examples: It's a *friendly* little diner where everyone knows your name.
The office has a relaxed, *friendly* atmosphere.

senses.gloss: On your own side in a fight or a war.
examples: The soldier was killed by *friendly* fire.
The damaged plane made it back to a *friendly* airfield.

senses.gloss: Done for fun or in a spirit of goodwill, not as serious competition.
examples: It's just a *friendly* game — nobody's keeping score.
They made a *friendly* bet on the Super Bowl.
A little *friendly* competition keeps the team motivated.

senses.gloss: Not harmful to something, or well suited to a particular group; usually after another word.
examples: We switched to environmentally *friendly* cleaning products.
The museum is very kid-*friendly*.
Is the hotel pet-*friendly*?

position: both — *a lovely view*, *The view is lovely*
contrast: There is no adverb *lovelily*: *She sings lovely* is wrong; say *She sings beautifully*. *lovely* has nothing to do with being in love or being loved: влюблённый is *in love*, любимый is *favorite* or *beloved*. It is far more frequent in British speech; Americans use it too, but *nice*, *great* and *beautiful* are more usual in casual talk.

senses.gloss: Beautiful or very attractive to look at.
examples: What a *lovely* view of the lake!
You look *lovely* in that dress.
It was the *loveliest* garden on the whole street.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant or enjoyable.
examples: We had a *lovely* evening — thanks for inviting us.
It was *lovely* to see you again.
The weather has been *lovely* all week.

senses.gloss: Of a person: kind, friendly and easy to like.
examples: Her parents are *lovely* people.
He's a *lovely* man and a great teacher.

position: both — *a lonely old man*, *He felt lonely*
contrast: *alone* means without other people — a plain fact — and it is predicative only: *She lives alone*, never *an alone woman*. *lonely* means sad because you are alone or have no friends: *You can be alone without being lonely*. *lone* goes only before a noun and means the only one: *a lone tree*, *a lone gunman*. There is no adverb *lonelily*; rephrase: *She sat by herself, feeling lonely*.

senses.gloss: Unhappy because you are alone or have no friends; or, of a time or a life, spent that way.
examples: After his wife died, he felt terribly *lonely*.
Moving to a new city can be *lonely* at first.
It was the *loneliest* year of my life.

senses.gloss: Of a place: far from where people live and seldom visited.
examples: The car broke down on a *lonely* stretch of highway in Nevada.
The cabin sits on a *lonely* hillside miles from town.

senses.gloss: Standing or moving alone, with nobody or nothing else nearby.
examples: A *lonely* figure walked along the empty beach.
One *lonely* light was still on in the office building.

position: both — *a lively debate*, *The debate got lively*
contrast: Pronounced LYV-lee, with the vowel of *five*, not the vowel of the verb *live*. Keep three words apart: *alive* = not dead, predicative only (*The fish is still alive*); *live* (LYV) = happening now or not recorded, before a noun (*live music*, *a live broadcast*); *lively* = full of energy (*a lively crowd*). *A live concert* is not recorded; *a lively concert* is energetic. There is no adverb *livelily*; say *in a lively way*.

senses.gloss: Full of energy; cheerful and active.
examples: Their kids are bright and *lively*.
At ninety, she's still as *lively* as ever.
He was the *liveliest* person at the party.

senses.gloss: Of a place or an event: busy, with a lot happening.
examples: The neighborhood has a *lively* bar scene.
The market gets *livelier* on weekends.

senses.gloss: Of a discussion or debate: full of strong opinions and eager talk.
examples: The proposal led to a *lively* debate at the town meeting.
The class discussion got pretty *lively*.

senses.gloss: Of the mind, interest or imagination: quick, strong and active.
examples: She has a *lively* imagination.
He took a *lively* interest in local politics.

senses.gloss: Of music or dancing: fast and cheerful.
examples: The band played a *lively* polka.
The song has a *lively*, catchy beat.

senses.gloss: Of colors: bright and strong.
examples: The kitchen was painted in *lively* shades of yellow and green.
A *lively* print can brighten up a plain room.

position: both — *a silly mistake*, *Don't be silly*; the 'bored silly' sense only after a verb
takes: *of* + a person + *to*-infinitive (judging the person: *It was silly of me to forget*); *for* + a person + *to*-infinitive (the plan makes no sense: *It's silly for us to take two cars*)
contrast: There is no adverb *sillily* in normal use: say *in a silly way*, or use a linking verb: *Stop acting silly*. *silly* is milder and friendlier than *stupid*: calling an idea *silly* is teasing, calling it *stupid* is an insult. To judge a person, the pattern is *It was silly of you*, not *silly from you*.

senses.gloss: Showing poor judgment; foolish.
examples: It was a *silly* mistake, and it cost us the game.
Don't be *silly* — of course you can come.
That's the *silliest* excuse I've ever heard.

senses.gloss: Playful and not serious, in a way meant to be funny.
examples: The kids made *silly* faces for the camera.
We all wore *silly* hats to the party.
He gets *sillier* the more tired he is.

senses.gloss: Small and unimportant; not worth worrying about.
examples: They had a fight over something *silly*.
It's just a *silly* little gift.

senses.gloss: Into a dazed or helpless state; only after verbs such as bore, scare and laugh.
examples: The lecture bored me *silly*.
The movie scared the kids *silly*.
We laughed ourselves *silly*.

position: both — *an ugly building*, *The building is ugly*
contrast: There is no adverb *uglily*: say *in an ugly way*. Said of a person, *ugly* is much harsher than Russian некрасивый; Americans soften it to *not very attractive* or *plain*. In *turn ugly* and *get ugly* it means dangerous or violent, not unattractive: *The protest turned ugly*.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant to look at.
examples: They painted the house an *ugly* shade of brown.
Honestly, I think the new stadium is *ugly*.
That's the *ugliest* sweater I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Of a situation or mood: unpleasant and threatening, likely to turn violent.
examples: Things got *ugly* when the police arrived.
There was an *ugly* scene outside the bar.
The crowd was in an *ugly* mood.

senses.gloss: Morally unpleasant; cruel or offensive.
examples: Someone started an *ugly* rumor about her.
The trial exposed an *ugly* side of the town's history.

position: both — *an elderly neighbor*, *My parents are elderly now*
comparison: more/most — *more elderly*, *most elderly*, both rare; *very elderly* is the usual way to grade it
contrast: *elderly* is a polite word for people who are old; *old* is plainer and can sound blunt about a person, and many Americans now prefer *older* (*older adults*) or *senior*. It is not a comparative: *my older brother* or *my elder brother* is старший брат, never *my elderly brother*. It is not an adverb either. *The elderly* (пожилые люди as a group) is a noun use.

senses.gloss: Of a person: old; a polite word.
examples: An *elderly* woman asked me to help with her bags.
The program delivers hot meals to *elderly* residents.
Her father is *elderly* and can't drive anymore.

senses.gloss: Of a thing: old and no longer working well; used humorously.
examples: He still drives an *elderly* Buick.
Our *elderly* laptop takes five minutes to start up.

position: both — *costly repairs*, *The repairs were costly*
contrast: For prices in stores and restaurants, *expensive* is the everyday word: *an expensive restaurant*, not usually *a costly restaurant*. *costly* is more formal and goes with repairs, delays, lawsuits and mistakes, where it often means causing loss: *a costly error* = ошибка, которая дорого обошлась. There is no adverb *costlily*.

senses.gloss: Costing a lot of money.
examples: The old roof needed *costly* repairs.
Treating the disease is extremely *costly*.
Flying turned out to be *costlier* than driving.

senses.gloss: Causing a serious loss, damage or suffering.
examples: Leaving the door unlocked was a *costly* mistake.
The delay proved *costly* for the company.
The fumble was the *costliest* error of the game.

position: both — *a deadly virus*, *The virus is deadly*; *deadly enemies* only before a noun
contrast: *deadly* = able to kill (*a deadly disease*, смертельный). *deathly* = like death (*a deathly silence*, *deathly pale*, мертвенный). *dead* = no longer alive. Before another adjective, *deadly* is an adverb meaning completely (*deadly serious*, *deadly dull*) — that use belongs to the adverb dictionary. In *the seven deadly sins* (семь смертных грехов) it means fatal to the soul, not to the body. There is no *deadlily*.

senses.gloss: Able or likely to cause death.
examples: Some wild mushrooms are *deadly*.
Fentanyl is far *deadlier* than heroin.
It was the *deadliest* hurricane in fifty years.

senses.gloss: Of enemies or a conflict: extreme and aiming to destroy the other side.
examples: The two gangs were *deadly* rivals.
They had been *deadly* enemies since high school.

senses.gloss: Extremely accurate or effective.
examples: He's a *deadly* shooter from three-point range.
She hit the target with *deadly* accuracy.

senses.gloss: Complete or total; with a few nouns such as silence and earnest.
examples: A *deadly* silence fell over the room.
She was in *deadly* earnest about quitting.

senses.gloss: Very boring; informal.
examples: The first hour of the movie is *deadly*.
Budget meetings can be absolutely *deadly*.

position: both — *a cowardly act*, *It was cowardly*
contrast: *coward* is the noun, so it needs an article: *He's a coward* or *He's cowardly*, never *He is coward*. Though it ends in *-ly*, *cowardly* is not an adverb in modern English: *He ran away like a coward*, not *He ran away cowardly*.

senses.gloss: Lacking courage; too afraid to face danger or difficulty.
examples: He was too *cowardly* to tell her the truth himself.
Don't be so *cowardly* — just go talk to her.
It was the *most cowardly* thing I've ever seen anyone do.

senses.gloss: Of an act: done so as to avoid risk to yourself, often by attacking people who cannot fight back.
examples: The mayor called the bombing a *cowardly* attack on innocent people.
Breaking up by text is a *cowardly* way to end things.

position: both — *orderly rows*, *The room was neat and orderly*
contrast: There is no adverb form: *Leave the building orderly* is wrong; say *in an orderly way* or *in an orderly fashion*. *An orderly* (санитар в больнице) is a noun. The legal phrase *disorderly conduct* (нарушение общественного порядка) is common in American news.

senses.gloss: Neatly arranged, with everything in its place.
examples: Her desk is always neat and *orderly*.
The books were lined up in *orderly* rows.

senses.gloss: Calm and well behaved, without confusion or disorder.
examples: Please leave the building in an *orderly* fashion.
The protest was peaceful and *orderly*.
The transfer of power was *more orderly* than people expected.

senses.gloss: Of a person, a mind or a way of life: organized, and following a regular system.
examples: She has a very *orderly* mind.
He lived a quiet, *orderly* life.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a timely reminder*; also *The warning was timely*
contrast: *timely* is not an adverb: *Please pay timely* is wrong; say *pay on time* or, in formal writing, *in a timely manner*. The opposite *untimely* is mostly met in *an untimely death* (безвременная смерть). Russian актуальный is often *timely* or *topical* — never *actual*, which means фактический.

senses.gloss: Done or happening at the right time, or without delay.
examples: Please respond in a *timely* manner.
We appreciate your *timely* payment.
Thanks for the *timely* reminder — I almost forgot.

senses.gloss: Dealing with something that matters right now; topical.
examples: Her book on artificial intelligence couldn't be *more timely*.
The documentary is especially *timely* in an election year.

position: both — *motherly advice*, *She was very motherly toward the new nurses*
contrast: *motherly* describes warm, caring behavior like a good mother's. *maternal* is the classifying word for anything connected with mothers: *maternal health*, and *my maternal grandmother* (бабушка по матери), never *my motherly grandmother*. There is no adverb: *She looked after him in a motherly way*.

senses.gloss: Kind, warm and protective, like a good mother.
examples: An older, *motherly* nurse held my hand the whole time.
She's always been *motherly* toward the younger players.
Nobody in the office is *more motherly* than our receptionist.

position: both — *fatherly advice*, *The coach was fatherly toward his players*
contrast: *fatherly* describes kind, guiding behavior like a good father's. *paternal* is the classifying word for anything connected with fathers: *my paternal grandfather* (дедушка по отцу), never *my fatherly grandfather*. There is no adverb: *He talked to me in a fatherly way*.

senses.gloss: Kind, protective and ready to guide, like a good father.
examples: My boss gave me some *fatherly* advice about saving money.
He put a *fatherly* arm around the boy's shoulders.
The old coach was *more fatherly* than strict.

position: both — *brotherly love*, *His concern was purely brotherly*
contrast: *fraternal* is the formal, classifying word: *fraternal twins* (разнояйцевые близнецы), *a fraternal organization*. For sisters the word is *sisterly*. There is no adverb: *He treated me like a brother*.

senses.gloss: Showing the love, loyalty or support expected between brothers.
examples: Philadelphia calls itself the City of *Brotherly* Love.
He gave his younger teammate a *brotherly* slap on the back.
Their rivalry was *more brotherly* than bitter.

position: both — *a scholarly journal*, *The book is scholarly but easy to read*
contrast: Russian научный splits in English. *scientific* is about the sciences and their methods (*a scientific experiment*); *scholarly* is about serious academic research in any field, especially the humanities (*a scholarly book on Tolstoy*); *academic* is about universities in general. In American English a *scholar* is учёный or a student with a scholarship, never a schoolchild.

senses.gloss: Of writing or work: based on serious academic research.
examples: The article appeared in a *scholarly* journal.
The book is *scholarly* but still easy to read.
It's the *most scholarly* biography of Lincoln to date.

senses.gloss: Of a person: having a lot of knowledge from serious study, and fond of study.
examples: He was a quiet, *scholarly* man who read Greek for fun.
Her *scholarly* manner made the students take her seriously.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a leisurely lunch*; also *The pace was leisurely*
contrast: Unlike most *-ly* adjectives, it is also an adverb: *They strolled leisurely along the river* is correct but bookish, and Americans usually say *at a leisurely pace*. Most Americans say LEE-zhur-lee; LEZH-ur-lee is also heard in the US, and LEZH-uh-lee is British. *leisurely* is about speed, not free time: свободное время is *free time* or *leisure time*.

senses.gloss: Done slowly and in a relaxed way, without hurrying.
examples: We took a *leisurely* walk along the beach.
Sunday breakfast is always a *leisurely* affair at our house.
The second half of the trip was *more leisurely*.

position: both — *heavenly bodies* only before a noun; *The cake was heavenly*
comparison: more/most — *more heavenly* in the 'delightful' sense; not gradable when it means 'of heaven'
contrast: *A heavenly body* is a star, planet or moon (небесное тело), not a beautiful person. Russian небесный is *heavenly* mainly in religion and in *heavenly bodies*; for the color of the sky say *sky blue*, and science uses *celestial*. In everyday speech *heavenly* is mostly about food, smells and comfort: *That bed is heavenly*.

senses.gloss: Of or from heaven, in religion; or in the sky, in the phrase heavenly bodies.
examples: The choir sang of angels and the *heavenly* host.
Our *heavenly* Father, hear our prayer.
Galileo studied the moons of Jupiter and other *heavenly* bodies.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant; delightful.
examples: This chocolate cake is *heavenly*.
After the long hike, a hot shower felt *heavenly*.
I can't imagine anything *more heavenly* than a week at the beach.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a ghostly figure*; also *Her face looked ghostly*
contrast: Do not confuse it with *ghastly* (GAST-lee), which means horrible or very bad: *a ghastly accident*, *a ghastly mistake*. *ghostly* means like a ghost. Neither word is an adverb.

senses.gloss: Pale, faint or hard to see, like a ghost.
examples: A *ghostly* figure appeared at the end of the hallway.
The fog gave the streetlights a *ghostly* glow.
Under the hospital lights her face looked *more ghostly* than ever.

senses.gloss: Strange and frightening, as if caused by a ghost.
examples: We heard *ghostly* footsteps in the attic.
The wind made a *ghostly* moaning sound through the trees.

position: both — *worldly goods* only before a noun; *She was older and more worldly*
contrast: *worldly* does not mean мировой or всемирный. For those use *world* before a noun (*a world record*, *world history*), *worldwide* or *global*: *world-famous* (всемирно известный), never *worldly famous*. *worldly* is about material life (мирской) or experience of life (искушённый).

senses.gloss: Connected with ordinary material life and possessions rather than with religion or the spirit.
examples: The monks gave up all their *worldly* possessions.
He left all his *worldly* goods to his niece.

senses.gloss: Experienced and knowledgeable about life, people and society.
examples: She seemed so *worldly* to us small-town kids.
He was older and *more worldly* than the other students.
A year in Paris made her *more worldly*.

position: attributive only — *a daily walk*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *I walk daily*
contrast: The same spelling is also an adverb (*The museum is open daily*) and a noun (*a daily* — ежедневная газета). Keep apart *everyday*, one word and an adjective (*everyday clothes*, повседневный), and *every day*, two words and an adverb phrase (*I wear it every day*). *Daily life* and *everyday life* both mean повседневная жизнь.

senses.gloss: Happening, done or published every day, or every working day.
examples: She takes a *daily* walk after lunch.
There are three *daily* flights to Denver.
The manager sends us *daily* updates on the project.

senses.gloss: Calculated for one day.
examples: The *daily* rate for the rental car is $45.
Try to stay under the recommended *daily* amount of sugar.
The *daily* high was 94 degrees.

senses.gloss: Belonging to ordinary life as it goes on day after day.
examples: Phones have become part of *daily* life.
The pandemic changed our *daily* routines.

position: attributive only — *a weekly meeting*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *We meet weekly*
contrast: Also an adverb (*The magazine comes out weekly*) and a noun (*a weekly* — еженедельник). *biweekly* is ambiguous — twice a week or every two weeks — so Americans often say *every other week* or *twice a week* to be clear.

senses.gloss: Happening, done or published once a week.
examples: We have a *weekly* team meeting on Mondays.
She writes a *weekly* column for the local paper.
The *weekly* farmers market runs until October.

senses.gloss: Calculated for one week.
examples: His *weekly* paycheck barely covers the rent.
The show topped the *weekly* ratings again.

position: attributive only — *a monthly payment*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *We pay monthly*
contrast: Also an adverb (*The bill is paid monthly*) and a noun (*a monthly* — ежемесячный журнал). *bimonthly* can mean twice a month or every two months; *every other month* avoids the doubt.

senses.gloss: Happening, done, paid or published once a month.
examples: The *monthly* rent is due on the first.
The library holds a *monthly* book discussion.
I set up automatic *monthly* payments for my phone bill.

senses.gloss: Calculated for one month, or valid for one month.
examples: A *monthly* subway pass costs $132.
Her *monthly* income went up after the promotion.

position: attributive only — *a yearly checkup*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *The fee is paid yearly*
contrast: *annual* is the more common and more formal word, especially in business: *an annual report*, *annual income*. *yearly* is the everyday alternative, and it is also an adverb. The vowel is the one in *year* (YEER-lee), not the one in *early* (UR-lee).

senses.gloss: Happening once a year.
examples: Don't skip your *yearly* checkup.
The town's *yearly* fireworks show draws huge crowds.

senses.gloss: Calculated for one year.
examples: Her *yearly* salary is about $60,000.
A *yearly* subscription saves you twenty percent.

position: attributive only — *an hourly wage*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *The bus runs hourly*
contrast: The h is silent, so the word takes *an*: *an hourly rate*, not *a hourly rate*. American *hourly* workers are paid by the hour, as opposed to *salaried* ones who get a fixed yearly amount. Also an adverb: *The news is updated hourly*.

senses.gloss: Happening once every hour.
examples: There's an *hourly* bus to the airport.
The station gives *hourly* traffic updates.

senses.gloss: Calculated or paid by the hour.
examples: The *hourly* wage for the job is $18.
Most of the store's *hourly* employees work part-time.
Lawyers at the firm charge an *hourly* rate of $400.

position: attributive only — *the nightly news*; after a verb English uses the adverb: *The show runs nightly*
contrast: It means every night or every evening, not simply ночной. For something that happens at night, use *night* or *nighttime* before a noun: *a night flight*, *nighttime temperatures*. Also an adverb: *The show runs nightly*. It sounds the same as *knightly* (рыцарский).

senses.gloss: Happening every night or every evening.
examples: My parents never miss the *nightly* news.
The theater has *nightly* shows through August.
The *nightly* fireworks at the park start at nine.

type: age — a time word: near the beginning, or before the usual time
position: both — *an early train*, *The train was early*
takes: *for* + an event or a time (*early for the meeting*); *to*-infinitive (*too early to tell*)
contrast: The same form is also an adverb — *an early flight* (adjective), *We left early* (adverb) — and there is no *earlily*. *early* compares with the usual or planned time (рано, раньше срока); *soon* means a short time from now (скоро): *Come early* = приходите пораньше, *Come soon* = приходите поскорее. Before a time word it needs no *of*: *in early May*, *in the early 1990s*, not *in the early of May*.

senses.gloss: Near the beginning of a day, a period, a process or someone's life.
examples: I caught the *early* bus to work.
She moved to Chicago in her *early* twenties.
The disease is easiest to treat in its *earliest* stages.

senses.gloss: Arriving, happening or done before the usual, expected or planned time.
examples: You're *early* — the party doesn't start until eight.
We had an *early* dinner before the movie.
This year the first frost was two weeks *earlier* than usual.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the first stage of history or of the development of something.
examples: *Early* humans lived in small groups.
*Early* computers filled entire rooms.
The *earliest* European settlers arrived in the 1600s.

senses.gloss: Happening soon, in the near future.
examples: We hope for an *early* reply.
Please contact us at your *earliest* convenience.
Everyone is wishing him an *early* recovery.

position: both — *holy water*, *This ground is holy*; *a holy terror* only before a noun
contrast: *holy* is not the title of a saint: *Saint Peter*, *St. Nicholas*, never *Holy Peter*; a holy person is *a saint*. Three words sound alike: *holy* (святой), *wholly* (полностью, an adverb) and *holey* (дырявый). *Holy cow!* and *Holy smoke!* are exclamations, not this adjective. *holier-than-thou* means acting morally better than everyone else.

senses.gloss: Connected with God or religion; sacred.
examples: Jerusalem is a *holy* city for three religions.
The priest blessed the baby with *holy* water.
Mecca is Islam's *holiest* site.

senses.gloss: Of a person: deeply religious and morally good.
examples: Her grandmother was a *holy* woman who went to Mass every day.
He likes to act *holier* than the rest of us.

senses.gloss: Used for emphasis in a few informal phrases, such as *a holy terror* and *a holy mess*.
examples: Their two-year-old is a *holy* terror.
The kitchen was a *holy* mess after the party.

position: both — *a jolly man*, *He was jolly*
contrast: *jolly* as an adverb meaning very (*jolly good*, *jolly well*) is British and sounds old-fashioned or jokey to Americans. In American English the adjective is most familiar from Christmas (*a jolly old elf*, *a holly jolly Christmas*); in everyday talk *cheerful* is more common. There is no adverb *jollily* in normal use: say *laughed cheerfully* or *laughed heartily*.

senses.gloss: Happy, cheerful and friendly.
examples: Santa is usually drawn as a fat, *jolly* man with a white beard.
The waiter was a *jolly* guy who joked with every table.
He seemed *jollier* after a couple of drinks.

senses.gloss: Of an occasion: enjoyable and festive.
examples: The whole family had a *jolly* time at the holiday party.
It was a *jolly* evening full of songs and stories.

position: both — *smelly socks*, *The fridge is smelly*
contrast: *smelly* is always negative — it means the smell is bad, like вонючий, not like пахучий. For a pleasant smell say *fragrant* or *sweet-smelling*, or use the verb: *The bread smells great*. After the verb *smell* use an adjective, not an adverb: *It smells bad*, not *It smells badly*.

senses.gloss: Having a strong, unpleasant smell.
examples: Get your *smelly* gym socks out of my car!
The fridge is getting *smelly* — we need to clean it out.
Blue cheese is one of the *smelliest* foods I know.

position: both — *curly hair*, *His hair is curly*
contrast: English puts the adjective on the hair: *She has curly hair* or *She's curly-haired*; *She is curly* is heard but informal. *curly* means tight curls; *wavy* means loose waves (волнистый). In American computing, *curly brackets* are usually called *braces* { }.

senses.gloss: Of hair: growing in curls.
examples: The baby has *curly* red hair.
My hair gets *curlier* when it's humid.
His hair is naturally *curly*.

senses.gloss: Having a curved or spiral shape.
examples: The pig has a *curly* little tail.
We ordered a basket of *curly* fries.
The old sign was painted in *curly* letters.

position: both — *a bubbly personality*, *She's so bubbly*
contrast: *bubbly* as a noun (*a glass of bubbly*) means champagne or sparkling wine — a noun, not this adjective. For drinks, American English usually says *sparkling* or *carbonated*: *sparkling water*. Calling a person *bubbly* is a compliment (жизнерадостная), used mostly about women and girls.

senses.gloss: Of a person: cheerful, lively and full of energy.
examples: Our new receptionist is *bubbly* and chatty.
She has a warm, *bubbly* personality.
She's even *bubblier* than her older sister.

senses.gloss: Full of bubbles.
examples: Bake the lasagna until the cheese is hot and *bubbly*.
The kids love *bubbly* drinks.

position: both — *a chilly morning*, *It's chilly outside*
contrast: It sounds the same as *chili* (перец чили, the American spelling), but *chilly* means cold in an unpleasant way — somewhere between *cool* and *cold*. For a person, English uses *be*: *I'm chilly* or *I'm cold* (мне зябко, мне холодно), not *It's chilly to me*.

senses.gloss: Of the weather, the air or a place: cold enough to be unpleasant.
examples: It was a *chilly* morning, so I grabbed a jacket.
The office gets *chilly* in the afternoon.
Tonight will be *chillier*, with lows in the forties.

senses.gloss: Of a person: feeling cold.
examples: I'm a little *chilly* — can we close the window?
The kids were *chilly* after swimming in the lake.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly; not warm in manner.
examples: The proposal got a *chilly* reception from the board.
Relations between the two neighbors have been *chilly* for years.
